grupos.reason: It names a concrete path: a null `evt.destinationCalendar` skips the optional-chained push, so collective hosts' calendars are silently dropped from the event.
With multiple calendar references, the legacy no-credentialId branch now issues deleteEvent against every credential once per reference, causing duplicate or wrong-target deletes and errors.
The case-sensitive comparison lets a case variant of an existing attendee's email through as a duplicate attendee, which creates wrong data.

The comment names a concrete failure. Attendees are persisted before the unguarded calendar update, so if that update throws, the guests are saved with no emails sent, and a retry is rejected as a duplicate.

The case-sensitive comparison lets an existing attendee's email re-added in different case create a duplicate attendee row, and concurrent calls can do the same, which is a concrete data-integrity bug.
A hard-coded English tooltip is a minor i18n polish issue; functionality is unaffected and nothing breaks.

Salesforce now refreshes the token and writes to the DB on every connection without using refreshOAuthTokens, which bypasses credential sync and can overwrite the stored credential key with a mismatched shape.
A non-constant-time secret comparison on an unauthenticated credential-writing webhook is a concrete security weakness (timing leak), not a style concern.
With credential sync enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw fetch Response, but the axios-based caller reads `.data.error`, which is undefined and throws a TypeError, so the refresh breaks.

The JSDoc makes a concrete false claim, saying `appData.type` is the app slug when it is written to the credential `type` column. That misleads callers, which the test counts as non-nit, even though runtime behavior is unaffected.
It describes a concrete failure: an unguarded update in the catch block can throw, abort the loop so remaining reminders aren't processed, and make the cron return a 500.

It suggests constant-time comparison as hardening for backup code checks, but describes no concrete exploitable failure, and a remote timing attack on a short, rate-limited string comparison is impractical.
The component is misnamed `TwoFactor` but works correctly and is imported under the right name everywhere, so this is only a naming and readability issue.
It only asks to reword a copy-pasted console.error message to say 'disabling 2FA' instead of 'login'; behavior is unaffected.
The only in-diff consumer, getBaseConditions, wraps each condition in parentheses, and the reduce also wraps, so the precedence problem only arises for a hypothetical future caller.
The unreachable branches in getBaseConditions are harmless dead code, so removing them is cleanup and leaving them causes no incorrect behavior.
It asks to rename a stale spec title; the test still passes and nothing in production behavior is affected.
It points out a test that passes for the wrong reason (it checks nothing about hosts), which is a test-quality issue with no effect on production behavior.
A missing host param (or EmbeddableHost.new followed by valid?) leaves host nil, so sub! in before_validation raises NoMethodError and the request returns a 500 instead of a validation error.
The hard-coded 10MB client limit replaces the per-type setting, so non-image uploads like attachments bypass their real limit and the alert shows a wrong number.
Unescaped `request.referer` in an inline JS string, with only the host validated, lets a crafted referer path or query inject script (XSS).

It names a concrete failure, a FrozenError on frozen input, and a real side effect where the caller's string is mutated by the appended footer, so it is not a nit even though current callers pass fresh strings.
The substring-based origin check in postMessage handling accepts origins that merely appear within discourseUrl, which is a genuine origin-validation weakness rather than a stylistic point.
An unescaped feed URL is interpolated into HTML that is later rendered raw without cooking, which allows HTML/script injection (XSS).
The feed_polling_url and embed_by_username tests pass vacuously because feed_polling_enabled? defaults to false, so they cannot catch a missing guard and give false assurance.
A feed item with nil content makes `i.content.scrub` raise NoMethodError, which aborts the whole poll and skips the remaining items on every hourly run.
It names a concrete race, PollFeed and RetrieveTopic importing the same URL at once, where the second create! hits the unique index and raises an unhandled exception.
The Disqus import now makes an unprotected HTTP fetch per thread, so one dead or invalid link raises and aborts the entire import, which the old local PostCreator path never did.
The precompile list in config/application.rb omits embed.css and embed.js, so in production the embed layout's stylesheet_link_tag would raise an error and the embed page would break.
The public members endpoint now caps every group at 50 members and the public page has no pagination, so non-automatic groups with more than 50 members show a truncated list.
It describes a concrete failure: translations in jobs or mailers never load the fallback locales, so fallback lookups return missing-translation output.
Missing re-check under the write lock only causes redundant manifest reloads on a cold cache; results stay correct and no failure is described.
It asks for an extra test assertion (request size metric absent for CheckHealth/CollectMetrics), which is a test-coverage request with no concrete failure in the current code.
Putting the base logger instead of the request-scoped one into the context only drops name, kind and method fields from downstream log lines, with no functional impact.

The new `break` in join() skips terminate() for the remaining processes once the deadline passes, which leaves flusher processes running after shutdown. The old code always terminated them, so this is a concrete regression.

The added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched, so the test's wait for the flusher thread does nothing and the messages assertion can run before the flush, making the test flaky.

`end` duplicates the `start` expression, so slots that begin within working hours but end after them are wrongly treated as available, which gives incorrect availability.
The `===` comparison of dayjs objects is always false, and the inverted utcOffset sign can shift the override window, so slots can be wrongly accepted or rejected.
`end` is computed from `slotStartTime` and so equals `start`, which means slots that begin inside working hours but run past the end are not rejected, and that gives wrong availability.
`end` is computed from `slotStartTime` and duplicates `start`, so slots that run past working hours are not rejected and the availability result is wrong.
`end` is computed from `slotStartTime`, so the end-of-working-hours check is ineffective and slots that run past working hours are wrongly treated as available.
Comparing two dayjs objects with `===` is always false, so the start==end (unavailable all day) override case is never handled, which is a concrete logic bug.

The working-hours check rejects any slot that falls outside any single range on a day, so split-shift schedules lose valid slots. It also computes `end` from the slot start and compares UTC time with schedule-timezone minutes, so availability results are wrong.
